story.title: A failed question does not prove ignorance
paragraphs: A factual question can fail because the model lacks the fact or because that wording does not elicit it. Conversely, a prompt can produce the target string without asking the original question. The paper defines a model's knowledge boundary as the facts it answers correctly under at least one expression; estimating it needs a probe that searches wordings while preserving what was asked.

If “Canberra is located in which country?” fails but “Which country contains Canberra?” succeeds, a single template underestimates the model. An instruction to print the target country, however, would show no knowledge at all. The search must go beyond a fixed template without redefining success.

mechanism.title: Gradient search stays close to the original question
paragraphs: PGDC (projected gradient descent with semantic constraints) searches the continuous space of token embeddings, where gradients point toward changes that make an accepted answer more likely. The target loss lets the answer appear after some generated text, not only at the first output position, and uses whichever valid answer alias is most probable.

Two further terms keep the probe from being gamed. A semantic loss penalizes the L2 distance between the candidate's last-layer representation and the original question's, and a regularizer keeps embeddings near real vocabulary items. After each step, embeddings close enough to a token are projected back to it, so the result stays a readable question.

evidence.title: PGDC finds more true facts without forcing false ones
paragraphs: Baselines follow common evaluation practice: zero-shot (zero) and few-shot (few) prompting, and a discriminator format (dis) that asks whether a statement is true; the P- prefix counts a fact as known if any listed paraphrase succeeds. PGDC is highest on both true-fact datasets, PaRaRel and KAssess, for every backbone except Vicuna on PaRaRel. On the fabricated facts of CFACT (CounterFact) and ALCUNA, a sound probe should rarely elicit the false target; the discriminator baselines fail this test, which the paper links to models' preference for answering “true”.

Semantic preservation is imperfect: three annotators judging 200 PaRaRel samples find that 83.3% of LLaMA2's optimized prompts keep the original meaning, from 80.5% for GPT-2 to 86.2% for Vicuna. A representation-level constraint therefore cannot certify every rewrite.

demo.title: Which probes find true facts without forcing false ones?
demo.description: Pick a true-fact set and a negative control.
